'''Amanda Weltman''' (born 1979) is a [[South Africans|South African]] theoretical [[physicist]]. She co-authored a series of papers proposing "[[Chameleon particle|chameleon]] gravity" to explain the existence of [[dark energy]]. She is a professor and [[South African Research Chair]] at the [[University of Cape Town]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=DST/NRF SARChI Research Chairs in the Science Faculty {{!}} University of Cape Town |url=https://science.uct.ac.za/research/dstnrf-sarchi-research-chairs-science-faculty |access-date=2026-04-01 |website=Faculty of Science |language=en}}</ref>

==Education and early research==
Amanda Weltman was drawn to physics while she was an undergraduate student at the [[University of Cape Town]].<ref name=Nature>{{cite journal |last1=Nordling |first1=Linda |title=Amanda Weltman: Driving Force |journal=Nature |date=7 March 2013 |volume=495 |pages=29–30 |url=http://www.nature.com/news/from-the-frontline-30-something-science-1.12549 |access-date=21 December 2015}}</ref> Describing her attraction to being a physicist, she stated that "understanding the way the Universe worked was just about the coolest job anyone could have."<ref name=Nature/>

In 2007, Weltman completed her [[Ph.D]]. in [[theoretical physics]] at [[Columbia University]] in New York. She was supervised by theoretical physicist [[Brian Greene]].<ref name=Chant/> She also did post-doctoral research at the [[University of Cambridge]] as part of the [[Centre for Theoretical Cosmology]] founded by physicist [[Stephen Hawking]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.iol.co.za/news/south-africa/gauteng/sas-future-could-be-written-in-the-stars-1993897 |title=SA's future could be written in the stars |publisher=IOL |date= |access-date=29 June 2016}}</ref>

==Personal life ==
Weltman was born in 1979<ref name="nnmu">{{cite web |url=https://www.nmmu.ac.za/sams-ams2011/weltman.htm |title=Sams-Ams 2011 |publisher=Nmmu.ac.za |access-date=13 July 2016}}</ref> in [[Cape Cod]], Massachusetts, and moved to South Africa with her parents when she was two months old.<ref name=NEF>{{cite web |url=http://nef.org/nef-fellows/amanda-weltman/ |title=Amanda Weltman &#124; Next Einstein Forum |publisher=Nef.org |access-date=13 July 2016}}</ref> She spent her childhood in [[Johannesburg]] and [[Cape Town]].<ref name=NEF/><ref name=Chant>{{cite web |first=Ruth |last=Chant |url=http://allianceofwomenscientists.com/articles/component/myblog/remarkable-journeys-a-dr-amanda-weltman.html?Itemid=122 |title=Remarkable Journeys – Dr Amanda Weltman |publisher=Alliance of Women Scientists |date=12 December 2013 |access-date=29 June 2016 |archive-date=27 February 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190227182236/https://allianceofwomenscientists.com/articles/component/myblog/remarkable-journeys-a-dr-amanda-weltman.html?Itemid=122 }}</ref> She was a competitive [[gymnast]] as a child.<ref name=NEF/>

{{as of|2013}}, she lives with her husband, Jeff Murugan, who is a [[string theory|string theorist]] at the same university.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Professor Jeff Murugan |url=https://uct.ac.za/contacts/jeff-murugan |access-date=2026-04-01 |website=University of Cape Town |language=en}}</ref> They met in 1997<ref name=Nature/> and have three children.<ref name=Chant/><ref name=Nature/> She has stated that she was glad to be brought up in a family largely uninfluenced by [[gender stereotypes]], noting that exposure to gender stereotypes in adolescence is frequently a barrier for young girls from pursuing science.<ref name=Nature/>

==Research and career==
Weltman became known when she co-authored a 2004 paper titled "Chameleon Cosmology" with Justin Khoury, which proposed a theory to explain [[dark energy]].<ref name=Nature/> She was a 24-year-old graduate student at Columbia University at the time.<ref name=Nature/> Dark energy is proposed as an explanation for the accelerating [[expansion of the universe]]. Khoury and Weltman proposed the existence of a new force that drove this expansion, which changed depending on the environment it was in. It would be weak when particles were densely packed together, and strong when they were far apart.<ref name=Nature/><ref name=Young>{{cite web|last=Young|first=Monica|title=Is Dark Energy a Chameleon?|date=24 August 2015|url=http://www.skyandtelescope.com/astronomy-news/is-dark-energy-a-chameleon-0824201523/|publisher=[[Sky & Telescope]]}}</ref> Thus, the theory suggests that in regions where matter is relatively dense, the chameleon force is difficult to detect, but in empty regions of space, it acts to push bodies apart and expand the universe.<ref>{{cite web |author=Belinda Smith |url=https://cosmosmagazine.com/space/hunting-dark-energy |title=Hunting for dark energy &#124; Cosmos |publisher=Cosmosmagazine.com |date=7 September 2015 |access-date=29 June 2016 |archive-date=24 March 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190324144918/https://cosmosmagazine.com/space/hunting-dark-energy }}</ref>

The theory of chameleon gravity can be tested in a range of environments including in laboratory tests.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Merali |first=Zeeya |date=2009-05-29 |title=Dark-energy particle spotted? |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/news.2009.531 |journal=Nature |language=en |doi=10.1038/news.2009.531 |issn=0028-0836|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The first searches for dark energy in the laboratory were performed as searches for chameleons. In 2007, Weltman joined an experimental team at [[Fermilab]] on the GammeV experiment which has been designed to search for axion-like particles. The first bounds on chameleon gravity parameters were placed by this experiment in 2008.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Cho |first=Adrian |date=2007-06-29 |title=A Spare Magnet, a Borrowed Laser, and One Quick Shot at Glory |url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.316.5833.1838 |journal=Science |language=en |volume=316 |issue=5833 |pages=1838–1839 |doi=10.1126/science.316.5833.1838 |pmid=17600197 |s2cid=44940449 |issn=0036-8075|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The experiment was redesigned and rebuilt as a purpose built chameleon detector, the GammeV CHASE (Chameleon Afterglow Search Experiment),<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Chou |first1=A. S. |last2=Wester |first2=W. |last3=Baumbaugh |first3=A. |last4=Gustafson |first4=H. R. |last5=Irizarry-Valle |first5=Y. |last6=Mazur |first6=P. O. |last7=Steffen |first7=J. H. |last8=Tomlin |first8=R. |last9=Upadhye |first9=A. |last10=Weltman |first10=A. |last11=Yang |first11=X. |last12=Yoo |first12=J. |date=2009-01-22 |title=Search for Chameleon Particles Using a Photon-Regeneration Technique |url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevLett.102.030402 |journal=Physical Review Letters |language=en |volume=102 |issue=3 |article-number=030402 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.102.030402 |pmid=19257328 |issn=0031-9007|arxiv=0806.2438 |bibcode=2009PhRvL.102c0402C |osti=1893404 |s2cid=12327360 }}</ref> with first results constraining chameleon dark energy in 2010. These were the first experiments of their kind and were able to place the first direct experimental bounds on the theory. This work pioneered a new subfield of laboratory experiments searching for chameleon gravity, or dark energy more broadly, in the laboratory.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2012-07-11 |title=Searching for chameleons in the dark |url=https://mg.co.za/article/2012-07-11-searching-for-chameleons-in-the-dark/ |access-date=2023-07-16 |website=The Mail & Guardian |language=en-ZA}}</ref>

==Awards and distinctions==
* National Women in Science award for the Best Emerging Young Researcher in the Natural Sciences and Engineering,<ref name=NEF/> in 2009<ref name="nnmu"/>
* Meiring Naude Medal from the [[Royal Society of South Africa]],<ref name=NEF/> in 2011<ref name="nnmu"/>
* NSTF-BHP Billiton, TW Kambule Award<ref name=NEF/>
* Silver Jubilee medal from the South African Institute of Physics<ref name=NEF/>
* The University of Cape Town Faculty of Science Young Researcher award, in 2010<ref name="nnmu"/>
* The College of Fellows Young Researcher award, in 2010<ref name="nnmu"/>
*Inaugural Next Einstein Fellow Laureate, in 2016–2017<ref name="NEF" />
*[[South African Research Chair]] Award 2016–2020 Tier 2, 2021–2025 Tier 1
